Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

issues.explanation: The trigger set is mostly coherent with rape trauma (locked/confined spaces, sexual-violence comments), but sirens are hard to connect to the rest of this profile and trauma context. With strong Negative Appraisals↔Threat and links from both to Triggers, the triggers should plausibly cue the patient's threat meanings; sirens do not fit the sexual-assault/confinement theme represented by the other trigger and appraisal items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilant unsafe-world items (back to wall, staying alert to sleep) fit well, but 'taking too many risks' pulls in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile with the same immediate threat style. It also lacks support elsewhere in the profile, since no other items suggest disinhibition, anger, numbing, or self-destructive coping.

vignette: John, a 37-year-old African psychologist living in Los Angeles, has been struggling with symptoms that have gradually eroded his sense of safety and well-being since he experienced a traumatic rape. The event occurred at a professional conference where he was staying alone in his hotel room late one evening. John had been enjoying the gathering and felt safe until he heard a noise outside his door. Moments later, a man forcibly entered his room, leaving him feeling violated and helpless. Since that night, John has found himself hyper-vigilant and unable to feel at ease in any space he cannot control. This is particularly evident when he finds himself in a locked or confined room, such as the small offices he often visits for work-related meetings. The mere presence of being in a closed environment triggers intense feelings of fear and anxiety. John's back always pressed against a wall, ensuring that he has a clear view of his surroundings at all times. John's experiences have also led him to become increasingly guarded about any comments on sexual violence. During professional trainings or discussions where such topics are brought up, he feels an overwhelming sense of discomfort and panic. His fear is heightened in situations where men are present alone with him; the presence of a male colleague can trigger vivid flashbacks and intrusive thoughts. His negative appraisals have deepened over time, solidifying his belief that he has no future and that bad things will continue to happen to him. This hopelessness and helplessness have created a vicious cycle where his threat perception is constantly heightened. He struggles to relax even in safe environments because the idea of being vulnerable again feels overwhelming. The constant vigilance affects his sleep, making it difficult for him to fall asleep at night as he stays alert, scanning for potential threats. John's negative appraisals have directly influenced how he perceives and reacts to triggers. The feeling that others can see what happened to him just by looking at him exacerbates his anxiety in social settings. He often avoids eye contact or any prolonged interactions with colleagues, especially men, which has strained professional relationships over time. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has made John feel increasingly isolated and disconnected from his work and community. His occupation as a psychologist, once a source of pride and fulfillment, now feels like an environment fraught with potential triggers. He is acutely aware that his performance at work is suffering; he often finds himself distracted during sessions and avoids taking on new clients who might remind him of the traumatic event. What finally brought John to seek help was a particularly distressing incident where he experienced a panic attack during a professional training session. The presence of male colleagues triggered intense flashbacks, leaving him feeling exposed and unable to cope in public. Since then, John has been acutely aware that his current state is not sustainable; the hopelessness he feels is overwhelming, and he is most hoping for relief from these constant fears and the ability to regain a sense of control over his life. In summary, John's journey since the traumatic event has shown how deeply intertwined his negative appraisals are with his heightened threat perception and triggers. The cycle of feeling hopeless and helpless has intensified his vigilance and avoidance behaviors, creating a self-reinforcing loop that continues to tighten around him. His current state is one of acute distress, but he recognizes the need for support to regain control and find hope again.
